about.title: About
about.description: Physicist turned AI engineer — building systems that think and compute.
paragraphs: I'm Wei-Che, an engineer with a materials science background and two years of packaging process experience, and a strong passion for applying AI to everyday life. I graduated from the Department of Materials Science at National Cheng Kung University and earned my master's from the same department. During my studies I took several semiconductor electives, including "Principles of Semiconductor and Photoelectrochemistry" and "Micro/Nano Device Process and Design." In my master's I used first-principles calculations to study the catalytic and electrical characteristics of materials, and published three related papers.

After graduating, I worked as a bumping process engineer in wafer-level packaging, responsible for the sputtering tools, managing process parameters and monitoring tool data. My team covered the front-end PI, Cu, and dry-film layers, so I am familiar with how coating, exposure, development, dry etching, and sputtering tools operate. Working production-line shifts built my ability to analyze, make judgments, and solve problems independently, and gave me experience collaborating with the equipment and quality assurance teams. Beyond keeping the line running, I took part in sputtering tool issue handling, trial runs, and process optimization, helped write tool operation SOPs, and explored ways to optimize the chamber-cleaning process.

I am willing to help others and take responsibility. In college I served as vice president of a student club, coordinating club courses and recruitment outreach. In graduate school I was a liaison for international students in the lab. At work, handling production-line issues also strengthened my cross-department communication and collaboration skills.

As AI has developed, I have also focused on applying it to everyday problems — from automating the cleanup and analysis of RAW DATA at work, to building a personal knowledge base and software tools with AI. By folding AI into my life and work, I keep exploring ways to improve myself and optimize processes. I believe a good engineer doesn't just solve problems; they build systems that keep evolving.

items.title: B.S. — Materials Science and Engineering
details: Studied the crystal structure and related defects of semiconductor materials
Learned material analysis methods and their principles (XRD / SEM / AFM …)
Took semiconductor courses to understand common PN junction and MOSFET device structures
Undergraduate project: evaluated anthocyanin as a flow-battery material and found it degrades too easily for long-term use

items.title: M.S. — Materials Science and Engineering
details: Ran first-principles calculations with VASP on NCHC (National Center for High-performance Computing) resources
Cross-lab collaboration: partner labs synthesized materials while I calculated their catalytic properties
Used commercial genetic-algorithm software for machine learning to help build simulation parameters
Studied green-energy materials through simulation, published 3 journal papers, and attended the TACT and ABBS conferences

items.title: Bumping Process Engineer
items.description: Bumping process engineer on a wafer-level packaging line, responsible for line stability and issue handling for the front-end PI / Cu / DFM layers.
details: Served as the owner of 9 sputtering tools, responsible for recipe and process-parameter management, first-line handling of tool issues, and data monitoring after preventive maintenance (PM)
Evaluated extending the sputter chamber-clean interval, analyzing tool by tool how the interval affects wafer resistance; preliminary results showed room to improve tool throughput

On the team's rotating evening shifts, covered the front-end PI / Cu / dry-film (DFM) layers of the bumping process, monitoring and handling issues across sputtering, PI coating, exposure, development, dry etching, DFM lamination, and water-clean tools

When tools went down, assessed the condition of wafers inside the tool and specified how they should be dispositioned (continue, rework, send for defect analysis, or scrap), limiting WIP damage and getting the line back up quickly
Automated multi-tool raw-data processing and charting with Excel VBA, replacing manual per-tool tabulation and cutting about 50 minutes per tool failure
Revised the OPUS metrology tool SOP with expanded procedures and illustrations, now the reference for new-hire training and consistent operation across shifts

categories.name: Computational Materials
categories.intro: Used first-principles calculations during my master's to study oxide electronic structure and catalytic reactions; the results went into 3 SCI journal papers.

tags.name: VASP
tags.detail: Primary calculation engine. Used for structure relaxation and electronic structure of ZnO thin films and metal-nanoparticle / oxide interfaces.

tags.name: DFT

tags.name: Band Structure Simulation

papers.title: Machine-Learning-Aided DFT-1/2 Calculations for Bandgaps of Zinc Oxide Thin Films
papers.description: Combined the DFT-1/2 method with genetic-algorithm artificial neural networks (GANNs) to predict ZnO thin-film bandgaps. GANN predictions differ from the DFT-1/2 values by less than 5% and match experimental data closely.

papers.title: Catalytic Hydrogen Evolution Reaction on Surfaces of Metal-Nanoparticle-Coated Zinc-Based Oxides by First-Principles Calculations
papers.journal: International Journal of Hydrogen Energy, 2022 — IF: 7.2
papers.description: Used first-principles calculations to study the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) catalysed by Pt/Au/Ag nanoparticle-coated ZnO surfaces. Au/ZnO showed adsorption free energy closest to zero, while Pt/ZnO performed best along the Volmer–Heyrovsky pathway.

papers.title: Mg₂Fe₂O₅ Nanoparticle-Decorated Ca₂Fe₂O₅−CaFe₂O₄ Heterostructure for Efficient Photocatalytic CO₂ Conversion
papers.description: The study paired a Mg₂Fe₂O₅-decorated Ca₂Fe₂O₅−CaFe₂O₄ heterostructure with DFT calculations for photocatalytic CO₂ reduction. The calculations revealed a Type-II charge-transfer mechanism and accounted for the 81.7% CH₄ selectivity.
